text: You’ve been trusted with your very own client. At 8:40 he’s already calling: “You’re one of the new ones? Then get me someone senior.” Your reply?
On a call, the client calls you by the previous manager’s name for the fifth time. That person quit six months ago. Correct him or just answer to it?
6:50 p.m. The client wants a “quick” call to go over “a couple of small things.” There are twenty-three small things on the list. Agree?
Your mentor assigns your first solo client call and sits next to you with a notepad. The pen is already clicking. Call with him there?
The client sent design feedback: “Make it livelier somehow, but serious.” Ask him what that means?
The script says to use the client’s name three times a minute. The client is now suspicious and asks if you’re a robot. Stick to the script?
The client added you on his personal messenger “for speed,” and at 9:30 p.m. sends a photo of his cat captioned “also working.” Reply?
The client arrived an hour early and is already in the meeting room. You’re still taking off your jacket, slides unopened since last night. Start?
left: Ask him to wait with coffee

text: The client wants a 30% discount. Your limit is 5%. Your team lead is in meetings till evening, and the client wants an answer now. What do you do?
On a video call, the client forgot to mute and is telling a colleague you’re still “totally green.” You hear everything. Let him know?
You accidentally sent the client a draft with the note “check whether he’s an idiot.” It’s gone. Now what?
First shift on the support line. The headset smells like someone else’s coffee, and a queue of 47 calls is blinking red. How do you start?
The client asks when it’ll be ready. You have no idea, and a coworker behind you holds up three fingers. Three days? Weeks? Hours?
The client thanks you and emails your boss praising you. The whole team is cc’d. Coworkers are silent. How do you react?
“Hello, it’s me again.” The client calls for the third morning in a row with the same question. The answer hasn’t changed, and he doesn’t like it. Answer?
At your first meeting, the client asks about a contract clause you’re seeing for the first time. All eyes on you. What do you do?
Friday evening, the client writes “Urgent!!!” then goes silent. An hour later: “Never mind.” Reply anything?
You were given a “warm” client list. Half the numbers don’t exist; the rest ask you to stop calling. What do you do with it?
At a meeting, the client suggests dropping formalities and tells a joke. It’s not funny, and your lead is watching you. Laugh?
The client sent a gift: a huge fruit basket with a note to you personally. Coworkers are eyeing the pineapple. Share?
Your lead hands you “the toughest client” with the words “everyone cut their teeth on him.” His profile has three skull emojis. Take him?
The client wants the presentation “in a normal format.” You sent three formats; he wants a fourth you’ve never heard of. Figure it out?
8:10 p.m. The client sends an eleven-minute voice message. The first two minutes are about traffic. Listen now?
Your mentor says to “smile into the phone” on client calls. You smile so hard your cheeks cramp. Keep practicing?
The client complains you answered his email in forty minutes, not five. He tells your lead. Will you justify yourself?
right: Explain you were in a meeting

text: Evening, team chat: “Who handled client Petrov? He’s thrilled!” It was you, but the credit seems to be going to your mentor. Speak up?
A client showed up unannounced, and all meeting rooms are taken. He’s at reception with a box of samples. Where do you take him?
The client has stalled on signing for a week and suddenly asks: “Would you buy from yourselves?” Your answer?
The client invited you to his milestone birthday. Refusing is awkward; going means Friday night in a restaurant with strangers. Go?
Unknown number calling. Could be a new client, could be another service survey. You’re in the elevator. Answer?
The client found an error on the invoice and is loudly outraged. Accounting made the mistake, but he’s calling you. Who apologizes?
As he leaves, the client asks for your “personal number, just in case.” His “cases” happen daily. Give it?
Before the meeting, your mentor whispers: “Whatever you do, don’t mention deadlines.” A minute later, the client’s first question is about deadlines. Your move?
The client sent a photo of a spec handwritten on a napkin. Half the words are blurred by coffee. Ask again or decipher it yourself?
The client thanks you and promises to “recommend you to friends.” Half an hour later his friends call — six of them, all with questions. Answer all today?
You forgot to log yesterday’s call in the CRM. This morning the system marked you “ineffective” and notified your lead. What now?
At a meeting, the client pulls out a competitor’s deck and asks why you’re pricier. The script has no answer. How do you wriggle out?
right: Promise to compare and follow up

text: The client closed the deal! Your mentor suggests celebrating at a bar, but you have another meeting at eight tomorrow. Go?
A client left a review: “Politeness top-notch, understanding zero.” It’s up on the big office screen. Your reaction?
The client has rescheduled three times. The fourth time he writes: “Can we do it right now?” You’re in the lunch line. Agree?
In the evening, the client sends the contract: “see what I’ve changed.” He changed everything, including your company’s name. Deal with it today?
At stand-up, you’re asked to talk about your first client. As you speak, your lead corrects every other word. Keep going?
The client wants it “like everyone else’s, but special.” Deadline: tomorrow. One version or two?
The client wants a proposal “by end of day.” You’re one step from the door, jacket on. Go back?
left: Send it from home at 11 p.m.

text: Reception calls: a client is here who was “just passing by.” No meeting, no name in the calendar. Go down?
right: Ask a coworker to greet him

text: The client unexpectedly praises you in front of your lead and asks that only you handle him from now on. Your mentor looks sour. Your reply?
Right before month-end close, the client asks to delay payment “a couple of days.” Your first bonus depends on it. Agree?
On a call, the client thinks you’re an answering machine and says slowly and loudly: “CON-NECT ME TO A HU-MAN.” Your response?
At a meeting, the client accidentally spills coffee on your laptop. He’s apologizing in horror. The meeting is in full swing. What now?
Today your first client praised you, then a second said you let him down. Evening, on the subway, replaying both talks. What do you do?
right: Put on a show and let go

text: Today’s quota: a hundred cold calls. It’s 9:05, and you’re still looking for the “headset” button on this phone. How do you start?
You call a company, and a kid answers and asks you to wait for Mom. Mom is the very procurement director you need. Wait?
The person on the line politely hears your entire script, then asks: “Do you actually believe this yourself?” Your answer?
5:45 p.m. Your counter says 61 calls out of 100. Coworkers are heading home and invite you along. Stay to hit the quota?
The new script opens with “Don’t hang up, this isn’t an ad!” It’s an ad. Say it?
For the fifth time, the assistant says the director is “in a meeting.” You can hear the director laughing loudly in the background. Push harder?
Last call of the day: the person is so happy to talk to a human that he’s been describing his vegetable garden for half an hour. He won’t buy anything. Interrupt?
The team’s top seller offers to teach you his “magic phrase” if you bring him coffee for a week. Deal?
You dial a number from the list and reach your own aunt. She’s delighted and wants to chat about family dinner. Your manager is listening in. Now what?
At the team review, the manager plays your worst call “for training purposes.” Everyone hears your “uhhh” on loop. Your reaction?
Today you heard “not interested” 43 times and one “get lost.” On the way home, you want to lie down on the sidewalk. How do you recover?
Morning, first call. Your just-woke-up voice sounds like you’re calling from a cave. Clear your throat or dial right away?
The call list includes a company that closed five years ago. The number now belongs to a pizzeria, and the pizzeria is willing to listen. Pitch?
7 p.m. You finally reach a client who was unavailable all day. He says: “Go ahead, I’ve got five minutes.” You’re on your way out. What now?
The manager posted the call rankings. You’re dead last, with a sad face drawn next to your name. What do you do?
right: Draw the sad face a hat

text: A prospect asks where you got his number. Honest answer: “It’s a purchased list, we have no idea.” Your version?
The coworker next to you calls so loudly that your prospect asks if you’re at a bazaar. Ask him to keep it down?
On your last call, someone finally says “Yes, interested.” But they want a callback on Saturday at 10 a.m. Agree?
At the sales huddle, everyone chants “We dial, we sell!” It’s your first time; you don’t know the words or moves. Join in?
The person has listened in silence for three minutes. You’re not sure he’s even there, but occasionally he breathes. Keep talking?
The manager demands you smile on calls and puts a little mirror in front of you. Your reflection looks very unhappy. Look in the mirror?
Instead of listening, the person starts selling you a sales course. And he sells better than you. Hear him out?
Your mentor teaches you to “mirror” the other person. Today’s first client talks very fast, with a stutter. Mirror him?
You mixed up the cards and call the client “Anatoly Petrovich.” She’s Anastasia Pavlovna and informs you of it very coldly. Your move?
You notice a coworker hits his quota by dialing his own number and hanging up. The counter counts it as a call. Tell the manager?
First call of the day, and right away: “Yes, send the contract.” You’re not ready for success — you don’t have a contract template. Now what?
The sales team lunches together, comparing how many deals they closed. You have nothing to brag about. Sit with them?
The person on the call is an intern just like you, and also selling. You’re both reading scripts at each other. What next?
Evening party in the sales chat: someone closed a big deal. Everyone’s sending fire emojis. Your day: zero. Join in?
The manager proposes a “contest”: first to twenty calls picks Friday’s pizza. Your rival is the team veteran. What do you do?
The prospect asks you to email everything. You know “email it to me” means “go away.” Keep pushing?
You got the time zone wrong and woke a client in Vladivostok at 2 a.m. He politely asks if you’re okay. Your move?
Your headset has hissed all morning; clients sound like they’re under a pillow. IT promises a new one “by Thursday.” It’s Monday. What do you pick?
The client asks about something not in the script. He seems to know more about the product than you. Admit it?
The manager listens to your calls on a second headset and writes notes on sticky notes. He’s running out of sticky notes. How do you carry on?
right: Ask for a review after shift

text: In the evening, you call through the “rejected” list. One of them says: “I liked you yesterday, let’s meet.” At 8 a.m. What now?
You rehearse your script aloud on the subway, and an old lady next to you asks with interest where she can buy your service. Tell her?
You’re interrupted: “You’re the third person from your company today.” Seems coworkers used the same list. What do you say?
At day’s end, the manager asks why your conversion rate is zero. You honestly don’t know. Answer?
The team rings a bell for every deal. All week, your bell hasn’t rung once. A coworker suggests ringing it “for the vibes.” What do you do?
The client wants the price now, without “all those needs questions.” The script forbids quoting a price before minute five. Say it?
You hit a phone menu so long that by “press nine” you’ve forgotten why you called. Fight through to a human?
At home, out of habit, you answer the phone: “Good evening, this is the company…” It’s your mom. She’s mildly shocked. How do you recover?
First number on the list is marked “DO NOT CALL!!! BITES.” The manager says it’s “an old joke.” Call?
The client agrees to meet, but only if you come in person to his out-of-town office, forty minutes by train. Go?
A coworker offers to swap lists: your “warm” one for his “promising” one. His list has “archive” in the name. Swap?
In the evening, you reach someone who once did cold sales himself. He listens, sighs, and buys “out of solidarity.” Your reaction?
The manager suggests calling standing up — “it makes your voice more confident.” An hour later your legs ache, and your voice is the same. Keep standing?
The client asks you to “call back in six months.” The CRM can’t set a reminder more than a month out. What do you do?
You dream you’re calling a client, and the client is your alarm clock. The alarm declines your offer. You wake at 3 a.m. Now what?
9:02. “Please do a little spreadsheet by ten, it’s a five-minute job.” It has four tabs and links to files you can’t access. Take it on?
The analyst asks you to “quickly” export a year of data by 3 p.m. The export has been loading for forty minutes and shows 3%. What now?
5:58 p.m. A task lands with “by morning.” Your lead’s morning starts at 7:00; yours at 9:30. When will you do it?
You need to print and bind forty copies for a meeting in twenty minutes. The printer does a page a minute. Your plan?
The marketer wants a photo for a post in ten minutes: “Something positive but not cliché.” What do you pick?
right: Search half an hour for perfect

text: You’ve got three urgent tasks from three different people. All are “top priority.” Who do you ask about priorities?
Leaving for the day, your lead tosses out: “Sketch some talking points by morning, nothing complicated.” Topic: the company’s five-year strategy. What do you do?
The weekly report is due at 10:00. Overnight, the template was updated — forty required fields instead of ten. Fill them all?
right: Do the key ones and flag it

text: A coworker asks you to proofread his deck “five minutes before the meeting.” It’s 63 slides in 15-point font. What do you choose?
Accounting calls: the expense report must be in “right now” or your taxi won’t be reimbursed. The receipts are in your winter coat at home. What do you say?
7:30 p.m. Your lead writes: “Fix one comma in the contract, the client’s waiting.” The contract is on your work computer; you’re home. Your response?
right: Ask a coworker at the office

text: The morning call moved an hour earlier, and you promised to “finish the slides in the morning.” Twenty minutes to go. Your move?
You need to send an event invite to a hundred people in half an hour. Email blocks more than twenty messages an hour. Your plan?
Your lead asks you to translate a letter into English “in about ten minutes.” Your English peaked at a school contest. Admit it?
Friday, 5:50 p.m. You’re told to prepare gift bags for clients by Monday. No bags, no gifts, no budget. What now?
You set a 25-minute Pomodoro timer to focus. During it, four people came over with “quick questions.” What next?
You urgently need a certificate for a tender. It ships at 3:00; it’s 2:20. One person issues it, and he’s at lunch. What do you do?
The designer wants the layout approved in twenty minutes. You haven’t received the client’s edits, and the layout has last year’s date. Approve?
At 8 p.m. your lead writes “do a little report by morning,” and at 11 p.m.: “no, never mind.” You’re halfway done. How do you react?
The office manager needs every employee’s signature on a greeting card by 9 a.m. It’s 8:40, and three people are in. How do you collect them?
A coworker forgot to do his part of a task, and now it’s on you, due in an hour. He’s already gone on sick leave. Do it for him?
The lawyer wants three contracts cross-checked by 4 p.m. Each is eighty pages of fine print. It’s 3:05. What do you do?
5:59 p.m. “Please fix the numbers in the spreadsheet, it’ll take two minutes.” Two minutes become an hour and a half. Where do you stop?
Panic in the project chat: “Does anyone know where the final version of the deck is?” You seem to have the final one — but you have four. Your move?
Fifteen minutes before the presentation, your lead asks to “add a couple of charts so it looks solid.” There’s no data for charts. Your move?
A courier comes for documents in ten minutes. They’re in the safe, and the key is with the accountant, who’s at the dentist. Your plan?
You’re heading out when a coworker asks you to help print “a couple of pages.” The printer jammed and wants a restart. Will you rescue her?
In the morning you get a task “by lunch”; an hour later you’re asked why it isn’t done. In your lead’s view, lunch is at eleven. Your reaction?
You found a formula error that makes the whole quarterly spreadsheet wrong. It’s due in twenty minutes. What now?
right: Report it and ask for time

text: The project manager gave you a task for Monday, but Friday morning asked for it “today, if possible.” Is it possible?
9:15 p.m. A coworker writes: “Remember where we saved the report file? It’s due in the morning.” You vaguely remember. Join the search?
right: Give a hint and log off

text: Your lead, from the doorway: “Is the slide I mentioned yesterday ready?” You remember no slide. Your answer?
In the tracker, you’re assigned a task due “yesterday.” It was created this morning. Do it or ask questions?
The office manager wants a room for thirty people tomorrow, found within half an hour. Every venue in town is booked for a conference. Where do you look?
Your lead goes on vacation and leaves you a list of “small things” for the week. Two pages, double-sided. Take it all?
Your alarm didn’t go off, and an urgent report is due at 9:30. It’s 9:05; the report is on your work computer. Plan?
“Make it look nice,” your lead says, and leaves for two hours. Nobody knows what “nice” means. What do you do?
A coworker asks you to cover his call in five minutes: “Just listen in.” On the call, you’re the first one asked to speak. Your choice?
You spent all day on small urgent tasks and didn’t do a single important one. It’s evening. Stay and do one?
“I need three promo ideas for stand-up.” Stand-up is in twelve minutes. You have one idea: a cookie discount in the cafeteria. Now what?
Supplies needs the stationery order by 2 p.m., or the next delivery is a month out. The team ran out of pens yesterday. How many to order?
Your lead cancels a task you’ve worked on for three days and gives you a new one — “also urgent.” Argue?
In the evening, the team chat asks for a volunteer to prepare a summary for the director by morning. Silence. The pause drags on. Your move?
You open your inbox: twenty emails marked “Urgent.” Eight are about a missing mug. Where do you start?
You’re asked for a “half-page” memo. An hour later your lead adds: “And the appendices.” There are seven. Can you manage?
A coworker begs you to watch his computer until an export finishes: “Twenty minutes, tops.” It’s been an hour and a half. Your call?
Your lead thanks you for a quick job and immediately hands you another “since you’re so good at this.” How do you react?
Deadline day, and you got up at six to get it all done. At 6:15 you find yourself cleaning the fridge. What next?
Your urgent report is done an hour early. Your lead didn’t ask for it early. Send now or hold it till the deadline?
You hit every deadline this week but you’re so tired you can’t remember your subway stop. How do you celebrate?
For three days you’ve nodded at stand-up whenever someone says “capex.” You still don’t know what it is, and it’s too late to ask. Now what?
Your mentor explained the task in thirty seconds and left. You caught one word: “urgent.” Chase him down the hall?
You’ve spent an hour on a spreadsheet formula. A coworker glances over: “It’s just a VLOOKUP.” You don’t know what that is. Admit it?
6:30 p.m. You still don’t get how to fill in the report. Everyone’s gone except the stern senior specialist. Approach him?
At stand-up, the lead asks: “Everyone clear on the task?” All nod. You don’t get it, but you nodded on autopilot. What next?
You ask the group chat how to request vacation, then see the answer pinned since last year. Delete your question?
Third trip this week to the sysadmin with the same problem. He sighs the moment he sees you. Go again?
All day you pretended to understand the new system. Tomorrow you have to close your first deal in it. Tonight’s your last chance. What do you do?
A senior coworker offers: “If anything’s unclear, just ask.” Five minutes later you have twelve unclear things. How many do you ask?
Your lead asks for a pivot table. You’ve never made one. He’s waiting for “Can you handle it?”
You asked a coworker how to send an invoice. He explained so fast and with so many acronyms it got even more confusing. Ask again?
In the evening you recall saying “Yes, I’m aware” three times today about things you weren’t aware of. Your conscience stirs. What do you do?
The new-hire handbook says: “Don’t hesitate to ask questions.” Below, in fine print: “FAQ answers are in the 200-page knowledge base.” Where do you go?
Your mentor is on vacation, and you’re stuck on a task. His messenger status says “online.” Message him?
A coworker from the next department mistook you for a presentation expert and asked for advice. You’re not an expert. What do you do?
You finished a task but aren’t at all sure it’s right. Send it to your lead, or show a coworker first?
The new touchscreen printer demands “badge authentication.” Third time tapping your badge; the printer beeps. The line behind you grows. What now?
Your lead sent a task mentioning “CF by RC.” You’ve never seen this before. Ask him or dig yourself?
At a meeting, someone asks you about a project you joined yesterday. Everyone waits. Your answer?
A coworker texts in the evening: “Hey, did that task work out for you? Mine didn’t.” Admit yours didn’t either?
The new coffee machine has forty buttons labeled in Italian. There’s a line behind you, and you’re pressing everything. Admit defeat?
You notice a senior coworker made an error in a report. He’s experienced; you’re in week three. Tell him?
You’re looking on the portal for how to get a courier pass and spend half an hour wandering through “Values” and “Mission.” Ask the office manager?
Everyone around seems to have it all figured out. You feel like you’ll be exposed as an impostor any minute. How do you help yourself tonight?
right: Browse job ads, just in case

text: Your lead asks: “You’ve handled this client before, right?” No, never, but he looks hopeful. Your answer?
The coworker you keep running to with questions put up a sign: “Questions after 4 p.m.” It’s 11 a.m. What do you do?
You’re rewriting a client email for the fifth time, afraid of mistakes. You could ask a coworker to check it. But what if he thinks you can’t cope?
Your mentor texts in the evening: “How’s it going? All clear?” You have forty questions but don’t want to look clueless. Your reply?
You’re offered a two-week morning onboarding course. You feel like you’re managing fine already. Your move?
You can see you won’t make the deadline. Ask for help now, or hope for a miracle by end of day. Your choice?
A coworker complains to your lead that you “ask too many questions.” The lead calls you in for a talk. How do you explain?
You’re too shy to ask if you can leave at six. Everyone stays till seven. Tonight you have movie tickets. What do you do?
In one morning, the cleaner explains how the office works better than HR did in a week. Take notes on her advice?
Your lead casually asks if you understand the new bonus system. You’ve read the policy three times and understood nothing. Your move?
In the newbies’ chat, someone asks exactly what’s bugging you too. Nobody knows. Go ask the lead for everyone?
Your question at today’s meeting got a snicker. All evening you replay it. How do you get over it?
Your mentor offers daily ten-minute Q&A sessions. They start at 8:30, half an hour before work. Agree?
You asked a coworker for a contract template, and he sent his personal “All the Important Stuff” folder: 400 untitled files. How do you search?
Everyone at the meeting is talking “synergy” and “quick wins.” You’re writing the words down to look them up later. Your neighbor peeks at your notebook. Say what?
You stayed late again because you were too shy to ask for help with a report. The report is nearly done; you’re nearly dead. The lesson?
In the morning your lead says: “Don’t be afraid of mistakes, everyone learns.” In the evening, he yells over a typo. What to believe?
Your desk neighbor always helps, but after each favor tells you about fishing for forty minutes. You need help again. Your move?
The company chatbot answers every question with: “Please contact your manager.” You asked where the restroom is. What now?
right: Find it with a map app

text: Today, for the first time, you honestly said “I don’t know, teach me.” The world didn’t end. How do you celebrate?
right: Log it in your wins diary

text: At stand-up you’re asked to “share your progress.” Your progress: you finally figured out what “progress” means at this company. Your answer?
The analyst offers to teach you pivot tables, but only during lunch. You’ve been hungry since morning. What now?
A senior coworker grumbles: “In my day, we figured it out ourselves.” Then sits down and patiently explains. How do you thank him?
All day you were afraid to ask if you understood the task right. In the evening: you didn’t, it’s all wasted. Tomorrow?
Your mentor asked you to keep a question list and bring it daily. By 9 a.m., yours is two pages long. Bring it?
The new-hire HR survey asks: “How comfortable are you asking questions? 1 to 10.” Your honest answer is 3. What do you do?
You notice that yesterday you sent a client an invoice with an extra zero. He hasn’t replied yet. Call first or wait?
At the meeting, your lead is looking for whoever mixed up the dates in the mailing. It was you. Everyone’s silent. Raise your hand?
A coworker blamed his mistake on “the new hire.” You’re the only new hire, and you never touched it. Defend yourself?
You accidentally deleted the shared project folder. The trash is empty. It’s 7 p.m., and nobody’s noticed yet. What do you do?
In the morning you learn every figure in your report is in dollars when it should be in thousands. It’s already with the director. Your move?
left: Fix it and email the director

text: Accounting calls: you mixed up the bank details, and the money went to another company. It’ll be returned, but in a month. Who tells the lead?
You accidentally sent a voice message meant for your mom about soup to the work chat. Everyone’s already listened. Delete it?
8 p.m., your lead writes: “Did you send the client the old version?” You did. A messenger reply would sit there till morning. Answer?
Your mistake surfaced yesterday, and your mentor took the blame in front of the lead. This morning he acts like nothing happened. Thank him?
You found an error in the shared spreadsheet — a senior coworker made it six months ago, and every calculation since is wrong. How do you raise it?
The client is unhappy about a typo in his name on a certificate. Two hundred have already been printed. How do you fix it?
In the evening you reread an email you sent today and see you signed it “With love.” It went to the tax office. What do you do?
At stand-up, the lead says “someone” didn’t enter data into the system, staring at the ceiling. You’re not sure it wasn’t you. Your move?
You notice a coworker spent half a day redoing his work because of your mistake. He didn’t say a word. Your move?
You ordered forty boxes of paper instead of four. Movers are already carrying them in. Where do they go?
Your lead calls you in “to talk about yesterday.” You don’t know which thing: yesterday had three small slip-ups. How do you start?
You hit “Reply All” on a complaint about the office coffee. The recipients: the whole company, including the CEO. How do you recover?
right: Act like it was on purpose

text: You sent a hundred pages of vacation photos to the shared printer, and it froze on page thirty. The line is getting angry. What do you choose?
You promised a client something the company doesn’t do. He’s already happily told his director. What now?
right: Ask your lead to fix it

text: A coworker writes in the evening: “Don’t worry, everyone makes mistakes. Just don’t do it again.” You don’t know which mistake. Ask?
In the morning your lead says: “Your mistake yesterday cost the company money. But I believe in you.” How do you respond?
At an all-hands, you share the wrong file: your shopping list instead of the report. Everyone sees “chocolate for after the chewing-out.” Now what?
A coworker offers to “quietly” fix your mistake so the lead won’t find out. In return, you cover his Saturday shift. Your move?
You made a mistake, fixed it, and the lead didn’t even scold you. But all evening you replay the moment. What helps?
You forgot your pass at home and have called security three times this morning to open the door. The guard now recognizes you and sighs. What do you say?
Your mistake spawned a new “three approvals” rule. Now the whole team gets every email approved three times. Coworkers know where the rule came from. Your reaction?
You mixed up two clients and sent one the other’s proposal — with the other’s prices. Call both?
Evening chat: who left the kettle on? It boiled dry and set off the fire alarm. It might have been you. What now?
Your mentor tells you that in his first month he once sent a contract to the wrong client. You feel noticeably better. Share your own flops?
An internal auditor found an error in your documents and asks who taught you to do it this way. Your mentor did. Name him?
Your lead wants a written explanation for being late to a client meeting. You were late because his own meeting ran an hour over. What do you do?
You caused the project delay, but your lead blamed the contractor. The contractor is upset. Your conscience nags all evening. What do you do?
In the morning, the spreadsheet with your formulas suddenly shows revenue of minus $3 million. The director opens it in ten minutes. Your move?
A coworker pinned a printout of your report error on the wall, captioned “Masterpiece of the Week.” Lots of people are laughing. Your reply?
right: Ask him to take it down

text: The client found a contract error you missed. He tells your lead: “The intern must have checked it.” Your lead looks at you questioningly. Your choice?
Your lead wants to “break down your mistake” at the all-hands so “everyone learns.” You want to sink through the floor. Agree?
You scheduled an important meeting for February 30. The calendar accepted it. The attendees didn’t. It’s 8:50, and the meeting is “today.” Now what?
The sysadmin is hunting for who downloaded a virus disguised as “free presentation templates.” The templates were really pretty. Your move?
A coworker admitted his mistake at the meeting — and mentioned that you saw it too and said nothing. Everyone looks at you. Your answer?
In the evening you’re mentally drafting your resignation speech over a tiny mistake everyone has already forgotten. Stop?
Your lead thanks you for owning your mistake promptly and says it’s rare. Coworkers look tense. How do you react?
You sent documents to the wrong address. The courier is already taking them to another city. How do you get them back?
Your lead asks who’s responsible for an error in the deck. It’s shared: you inserted the numbers, a coworker made the charts. Who answers?
You accidentally reacted with a fire emoji to a message about someone’s hamster dying. Everyone’s silent. What now?
After yesterday’s slip, you woke up sure everyone will look at you funny. In the elevator someone smiled at you. How do you start the day?
You confessed a mistake, and your lead says: “No big deal, I didn’t even notice.” Now the whole team knows. Was it worth it?
A coworker loudly accuses you of losing his favorite pen. It’s tucked behind his ear. Tell him?
As he leaves for the day, your lead says: “Tomorrow we’ll discuss your work.” It’s unclear what he meant. Evening ruined?
The office manager is looking for whoever broke the meeting-room chair. You sat on it yesterday, and it creaked pitifully. Confess?
A client thanks you for the quick reply, and you realize you answered a question he never asked. Correct it?
Today is your first end-of-probation review. HR sent a six-page self-assessment due by lunch. How do you fill it in?
At your review, the lead asks: “Where do you see yourself in five years?” The honest answer is “on vacation.” What do you say?
The review form requires feedback from three coworkers. You’ve been here two weeks and know only two by name. Who’s the third?
Quarterly review tomorrow. You rehearse “I show initiative” in the mirror and realize you can’t recall a single initiative. What do you do?
Your lead has postponed your review for the third time. Now it’s “sometime next week.” Your raise depends on it. Remind him?
On the competency scale, you got “3 out of 5” for “strategic thinking.” You’re an intern in charge of printing badges. Dispute it?
A coworker asks you to write him a glowing review. You worked with him once, and he was an hour late. What do you write?
Your lead texts in the evening: “Tomorrow at your review we’ll discuss your strengths and growth areas.” Judging by the tone, there are many growth areas. How do you prepare?
Before your review, HR wants you to take a “leadership potential” test. Question one: which tree are you? What do you do?
At your review, the lead warmly praises you for a project another intern actually did. Correct him?
Anonymous feedback about you: “Eats apples too loudly.” No other comments. How do you take it?
Review done: “Good, but could be better.” You can’t tell if that’s good or bad. Mull it over tonight?
For your review, the lead wants six-month SMART goals. Your only goal so far: find out where the kettle is. Your move?
A five-person committee runs your review. Three you’ve never seen. One keeps yawning. How do you carry yourself?
The lead asks what score you’d give yourself. Every answer feels like a trap. Your choice?
Evening, interns compare scores in the group chat. Everyone got “excellent”; you got “satisfactory.” Post yours?
In the morning the lead says intern promotions are “frozen till next year.” Your review is in an hour. Is there any point trying?
HR offers you a “development plan”: courses, webinars, and mentoring. All outside work hours, in the evenings. What do you do?
At the review, the lead asks for your weaknesses. You say “perfectionism.” He smiles: “And for real?”
After the review, you got praise but no raise. In the evening you stare out the window calculating a month’s rent. What next?
Before his review, a fellow intern asks for your list of achievements “for inspiration.” Your achievements are very similar. Share it?
The lead praises you publicly: “Our best intern.” Next day, the other interns greet you noticeably more coldly. Your move?
The self-assessment asks which “company value you embody”: “Drive,” “Synergy,” or “Love for the Customer.” Your pick?
Late at night, the lead sends a draft of your review “for approval.” Your last name is misspelled. What do you say?
Review morning. You put on your best blazer, and it’s a size smaller than you remembered. No time to change. How do you react?
right: Take it off, go in a T-shirt

text: At the review, the lead unexpectedly asks what you’d change about how the team works. The team sits behind a thin wall. What now?
As part of a “360 review,” you’re asked to rate your manager. Anonymity is guaranteed, but the team is three people. How do you rate him?
After the review you were told you “lack proactivity.” All evening you think about how to be proactive, but ideas end at “come in earlier.” What do you do?
HR accidentally sent review results to everyone: you and your coworkers. The whole floor knows your score. Your move?
The lead says: “You’re doing well, but I want to see more enthusiasm.” You already smile till your cheeks hurt. Your reply?
A coworker confides that intern scores are decided in advance and the review is a formality. Yours is tomorrow. Believe it?
Evening, the team chat congratulates an intern on going full-time. You haven’t been offered that yet. Congratulate him?
Before the review, the lead wants a “fifteen-minute” presentation on your achievements. You have about three minutes’ worth. Your choice?
A committee member asks about a topic you’ve never studied. The others wait with interest. What now?
HR’s form asks for “the mentor who influenced you most.” Your mentor was on vacation the whole time. Your move?
Your review says “meets expectations.” You never figured out whose expectations. Spend the evening pondering, or at the movies?
First thing in the morning, the lead asks if you want feedback “honest or kind.” Your choice?
You’re offered a full-time job, but in another department with “slightly different tasks.” Slightly different means the warehouse. Accept?
Your KPI sheet has a metric: “ideas per month.” You have zero. The lead suggests you “just write something in.” Your reaction?
9 p.m., your lead writes: “Looked at your self-assessment. Let’s discuss.” Nothing else. You stare at the screen. What do you do?
The morning of your review, you’re tempted to call in sick. You’re fine, just scared. What do you do?
The lead compares you to last year’s intern: “He did three times more in a month.” How do you react?
For a good review, HR offers “non-monetary motivation”: a certificate and a photo on the honor board. No money. Your move?
An experienced coworker shares how she prepped for her first review: “I cried in the elevator.” Does that help?
In the morning, the lead says he gave you “excellent” but asks you to keep it quiet so as “not to upset the others.” Your choice?
Nerves made you lose your voice at the review. You’re whispering, and the committee leans in. Keep whispering?
The lead suggests “slightly tweaking” your self-assessment: removing “exhaustion” from the “well-being” field. What do you do?
You got your first-ever bonus for your review results. Small, but yours. What do you spend it on?
The lead asks if you remember the goals you set six months ago. You only remember that there were some. Your move?
At his own review, a coworker credits your help, calling you his “right hand.” The lead is surprised the right hand has its own tasks. What do you say?
You’ve been given your first intern. Timur arrived at 8:00 with a notebook, asking what to do. You get in at 9:30 and aren’t even awake yet. Your move?
The intern finished a task in ten minutes instead of two days. Suspiciously fast. Check it or celebrate?
Vika the intern asks why the team does things this way. You don’t know. You’ve only been here three months yourself. Your answer?
7 p.m. The intern won’t go home because you haven’t left. You haven’t left because your report isn’t done. Let him go?
right: Give him part of the report

text: Intern meet-and-greet day. Everyone has to share an “interesting fact.” Yours: you’re afraid of interesting facts. What now?
The intern politely corrects you in front of the lead: there’s an error in your report. She’s right. The lead looks intrigued. What do you do?
Your lead asks you to “do a bit of teaching” with the intern. Your workload stays the same. Take it?
The interns invite you to a bar to “celebrate week one.” You’re two years older than them all and one year junior in position. Your move?
The intern brings you coffee every morning and calls you “chief.” Coworkers start smirking. Ask him to stop?
The intern asks to leave early for a university exam. The lead is out. It’s your call. Your choice?
The intern enthusiastically pitched the lead an idea you discussed with him yesterday. It’s your idea. The lead is thrilled. What now?
Six months ago you were an intern yourself. Today the intern asked how you manage to “know everything.” You think about it all evening. Your move?
The intern came to work in a suit, and the whole office is in hoodies. She panics and asks if she should change. What do you say?
The intern accidentally forwarded your internal emails about a client to that client. Polite emails — mostly. Who apologizes?
Your lead asks your opinion on whether to hire the intern full-time. He’s diligent but slow. How do you respond?
The intern texts in the evening: “Sorry, I can’t come tomorrow, my cat is sick.” You don’t know if that’s allowed. What now?
The intern decorated your shared desk with string lights and stickers. It looks like a kindergarten. The lead is coming soon. What do you do?
The intern ate someone else’s lunch from the fridge, sincerely believing “everything here is shared.” It belonged to Tamara from Accounting. Explain?
The intern works slowly and very carefully. The task is urgent. Take it over or let her finish?
You catch yourself explaining a task to the intern with your lead’s phrase that used to drive you crazy: “Well, it’s obvious.” Now what?
The intern wants to “optimize” the department and has a thirty-point list. Point one: scrap morning stand-ups. Your move?
right: Gently talk him out of it

text: The intern asks how to ask the lead for a raise. You’ve never asked yourself. Your choice?
HR asks you to give the interns an office tour. You still mix up the floors yourself. What now?
The intern is collecting signatures for a petition to “introduce Pizza Fridays.” He wants you to sign first. Your move?
The intern has been late three days running. The lead asks you “what’s up with your mentee.” You don’t know. What do you say?
The intern asks a question every three minutes — forty since morning. You haven’t even opened your own work. What now?
Your lead praises your intern for excellent work and doesn’t mention you. You trained him for two weeks. Your reaction?
In the evening chat, the interns decide you’re “the coolest mentor.” You’re appointed to answer their questions on weekends. What now?
The intern burst into tears after a harsh email from the lead. She’s in a meeting room. You walk by with coffee. What do you do?
The intern broke the laminator trying to laminate a sandwich “to preserve it.” The office manager asks who was supervising him. Your move?
The intern offers to run a shared chat for interns and your team. It quickly turns into a meme swap. Your choice?
Your intern is leaving after the internship for another company, at a higher salary than yours. Evening, you stare at the wall. What next?
The intern made the morning presentation for the team. Half the data is wrong. It starts in ten minutes. What now?
Your lead decided the interns will lunch with you so they “integrate into the team.” Lunch was the only quiet time in your day. Your move?
The intern accidentally saw your search: “how to stop being afraid of your boss.” She nods knowingly. What do you say?
The intern calls in the evening: “Can I finish it tomorrow?” It was due today. You have to submit tomorrow. Your reaction?
The internship coordinator wants a “mentor diary” filled in every morning. Four lines a day of “what the mentor did.” What now?
The intern offers to automate your manual task. He’s already written a script. If it works, will you be unnecessary?
The intern asks for help with her thesis “for just an hour at lunch.” The topic: “crisis communications.” Ironic. What do you do?
A veteran coworker tells you in the evening: “Barely here a week, and already teaching interns.” It stings, but it’s partly true. Your move?
The intern suggests doing quick morning exercises together right at your desks. Your desk neighbor is already rolling his eyes. Your choice?
Your lead wants you to handle the next intern intake: reading résumés and interviewing. You have zero experience. What now?
The intern burned popcorn in the microwave. The whole floor reeks. She looks at you in horror. Your move?
The intern’s last day. He gives you a card: “Thanks for teaching me everything.” You’re not sure you taught him anything. What do you say?
In the morning you realize the intern works better than you. He comes earlier, leaves later, and remembers everything. Your move?
right: Ask him to try less hard

text: At a meeting, the intern loudly asks the “dumb” question everyone was afraid to ask. The lead frowns. Back him up?
The intern wants a “real” task, not spreadsheets. There’s only one real task — and it’s your favorite. How do you respond?
A meme about “the mentor who’s always busy” appears in the intern chat. Everyone’s laughing. Seems it’s about you. What now?
The intern was late because he “slept past his stop.” A week later you sleep past the same stop. He sees you rush in. What do you do?
Your lead says the intern will be hired if you vouch for him. You have doubts. Your move?
7:50 a.m. Mom calls to ask if you’ve had breakfast. You’re running for the subway with a sandwich in your teeth. Answer?
A childhood friend writes: “I’m in your city just today, let’s have lunch!” Your lunch is fifteen minutes at noon, with a meeting at 12:30. Your choice?
Grandma calls in the evening and spends forty minutes on her neighbor. You still have three emails and a raw dinner in the oven. What now?
right: Promise to call on the weekend

text: Your roommate took over the bathroom at 7:30 and is singing opera with feeling. You leave at 7:45 and haven’t washed up. Knock?
Your sister texts during work hours: “Urgent! Which dress is better?” Fourteen photos attached. Your lead is right behind you. Your move?
Friends invite you to Friday board games for the third time. You decline for work for the third time. The chat jokes that you’re “a myth.” What do you say?
Your partner made breakfast and wants to talk vacation plans. You’re running late for stand-up. How do you respond?
Mom calls right in the middle of your client call. Twice. Three times. What if something happened? The client is mid-question. What do you do?
A friend is celebrating a birthday at a restaurant. You arrive an hour late because of a report, and the cake is gone. How do you make up for it?
Your nephew sends a video: he rode a bike for the first time. You’re watching it for the fifth time in the elevator. Be late?
The family chat is planning who brings what to the country house on Saturday. You’re down for kebabs and a trailer. You don’t have a trailer. What do you do?
Your partner got tired of waiting for you and ate both dinners. You get home at 9:30 p.m., starving. How do you react?
At 6:30 a.m., Dad sends an article: “How to Become a Boss in a Year.” Captioned “This’ll come in handy.” Reply?
A friend invites you to the cafe across the street for lunch. You promised your lead you’d eat at your desk to make the deadline. Your move?
You promised to be at your little brother’s school concert at 6 p.m. At 5:40, your lead calls you over “for a minute.” Your choice?
Your parents decided to visit “for a week” and arrive Monday morning. You’re meeting them at the station at 7:00. What now?
A friend asks for help with his résumé at lunchtime, because “you work in an office, you know this stuff.” You don’t. Your move?
Friends threw a surprise party for your first month at work. It started at 7 p.m. You got free at 8:40. What do you say?
The cat lay down on the shirt you set out for an important meeting. It’s covered in fur now. Five minutes left. How do you react?
Mom asks by text: “When did you last have a proper lunch?” You think about it and can’t remember. Your answer?
Your partner suggests a “phone-free evening.” Right then, your phone buzzes with the team chat. What now?
left: Put the phone in a drawer

text: A neighbor in the elevator learns where you work and asks you to “get his nephew a job there.” You’re an intern on probation. What do you do?
A friend sends a beach photo: “Still at the office?” You are, it’s raining, and there’s a 3,000-row spreadsheet on screen. Reply?
left: Send a photo of the ficus

text: At dinner, everyone’s discussing your weekend plans. Your only plan: “sleep.” The family wants to go to the country house. Your move?
The neighbors’ daughter practices violin from 7 a.m. Today she’s especially inspired. Your alarm is set for 8:00. Your choice?
Your brother calls about a tax deduction. He’s sure that since you work in an office, you know everything about taxes. What now?
A friend invites you to yoga at 8 p.m. You can make it if you leave right now. Your lead is still here. Your move?
Mom sends a voice message: “You remember it’s Dad’s milestone birthday today?” You didn’t. No gift. What now?
A former classmate writes: “I’m a department head now. How about you?” You’re a junior specialist. Your reply?
Friends text: “We’re at the bar across from your office!” You’re finishing a spreadsheet. Through the window, you can see them having fun. Your answer?
Grandma packed you a container of meatballs this morning. The meatball aroma is spreading across the whole floor. Your reaction?
Your partner calls midday: “Remember what day it is?” You don’t. A very long, very expressive pause follows. How do you get out of it?
Mom needs help moving on Saturday. You promised your lead you’d finish a report over the weekend. What now?
The family chat wants a photo of your workspace “to see how you’re settling in.” Your desk is buried in papers and mugs. What do you do?
A friend who already owes you money asks for more. You just got your first paycheck and wanted new sneakers. Your move?
Your sister asks you to babysit on Friday evening. You’re so tired from the week that you need a babysitter yourself. Your choice?
Your parents ask when your vacation is so they can plan a family trip. You’re not eligible for six months. What now?
A friend shares news at lunch: she’s getting married, and you’re her witness. The wedding is on a weekday, mid-reporting season. Your move?
Your partner says you mumble “approved” and “for signature” in your sleep. Time for a change?
A friend writes: “Want to run a 10K with me on Saturday?” The last time you ran was after a bus. What do you say?
Your family asks if you’re coming to Sunday lunch. Your presentation is due Sunday. How do you respond?
Friends in the chat are debating where to celebrate New Year’s. Nobody asks you: “You’ll be working anyway.” What now?
Mom sends a “quick breakfast for busy people” recipe. You have to soak oats overnight, and you only remember in the morning. What do you do?
Your brother writes: “I need your signature at the notary, today before five.” You’re at work till six. Your move?
For the first time in a month, you visit a friend. Ten minutes in, you’re not talking about life, but about your boss. Change the subject?
The cat woke you at 5 a.m. demanding breakfast. You can’t fall back asleep. Three hours till the alarm. Your choice?
A friend is hurt you didn’t answer her message for two days. You saw it but had no time. What do you say?
Everyone at home is asleep, and you’re eating cold pasta over work emails. A note on the fridge: “We miss you.” What next?
In the morning, your partner asks what time you’ll be home. You laugh. Your partner doesn’t. What now?
Mom shows up at your office unannounced with homemade pies “to meet the bosses.” She’s at reception, waving at the guard. Your move?
You bought a membership at the gym next to the office to work out in the mornings. It’s 7:00, dark and wet outside. Go?
At lunch, you could walk in the park or sit in the shared kitchen where coworkers discuss TV shows. Where to?
Your guitar has stood in the corner for three months, ever since you started this job. Tonight’s free, but you only have energy to stare at the ceiling. What do you do?
You went to bed at 2 a.m. because of “one more episode.” The alarm rings at 7:00. You could store office supplies in the bags under your eyes. Your reaction?
A coworker invites you to the company running club. Tuesdays at 7 a.m., before work. Afterward everyone’s peppy and slightly suspicious. What now?
You signed up for art classes on Wednesdays. It’s Wednesday, and at 5:55 your lead asks you to “stay an extra half hour.” What do you do?
Sunny morning. You could bike to work — forty minutes — and arrive energized but a bit sweaty. Or take the subway as usual. Your move?
The team is putting together a squad for the company soccer tournament. You haven’t played since school. They’re one player short. Your choice?
Time to sleep, but you’re lying in bed mentally editing tomorrow’s presentation. It’s midnight. What now?
Your meditation app suggests a ten-minute morning session. You’re already five minutes late. Meditate?
HR runs lunchtime yoga in the meeting room. The instructor asks everyone into “downward dog.” Your lead is right next to you. What now?
You bought a book a month ago and read two pages. Tonight’s free, but your hand keeps reaching for the work chat. Your move?
The alarm went off half an hour early: you set it last night to do a workout. Now the idea feels like mockery. What do you say?
A coworker suggests lunchtime chess. Games last longer than the break. Your lead has walked by twice already. Your reaction?
You’ve long dreamed of dancing. The studio near home opened evening classes. They end at 10 p.m., and you’re up at 7. What now?
Saturday, 9 a.m. Your lead writes in the work chat: “Anyone free today? There’s a small task.” You’re in pajamas. What do you do?
You brought your swim bag to the office to go after work. It’s damp — you forgot to take out the towel last time. Your move?
Friday, 10:30 p.m. A coworker writes: “Still up? Want to discuss an idea for Monday.” You’re dozing off on the couch. Your choice?
You go for a morning run and meet your lead in the park. He runs too and suggests running together. What now?
A coworker found out you knit and publicly ordered a scarf. Now five more people want scarves. Your move?
Saturday, 7 p.m. An email from your lead marked “important.” Subject: “Thinking out loud.” Open it?
You woke at 4:30 a.m. thinking you forgot to send an email. You did send it; you’re just not sure. Get up and check?
The company sports club holds a plank contest right in the hallway. You last eight seconds. Everyone’s watching. What do you say?
Sunday evening. You feel the familiar dread of Monday. You still have a couple hours of freedom. Your reaction?
You used to brew stovetop coffee and read in the mornings. Now it’s instant on the run. Today you got up a bit early. What now?
A coworker brags he ran a half marathon over the weekend and asks what you did. You slept 14 hours. What do you say?
Sunday, 9 p.m. Your lead schedules a “quick 15-minute call” for Monday at 8:00. The invite is in your calendar. Your move?
Your fitness tracker reports you slept 4 hours 12 minutes, “sleep quality: low.” Thanks, tracker. Your choice?
A lunchtime interdepartmental chess tournament. Your team can’t field a full lineup without you. What now?
Tonight: finish the series you’ve waited all year for, or sleep early to be sharp for tomorrow’s report. Your move?
Saturday. The alarm went off at 7:00 out of work habit. Sleep more, or finally hit the farmers’ market?
A coworker invites you on an overnight mountain hike on Saturday. You wanted rest, but not in a tent. Your reaction?
You brought the work laptop home “just in case.” It’s 10 p.m., and it beckons from the desk with a blinking notification light. What now?
Your bike got a flat on the way to work. Two miles to the office, twenty minutes to stand-up. What now?
right: Get a taxi with the bike

text: You’re invited to company volleyball after work. You last saw a ball in school. Coworkers promise “not to hit hard.” What do you do?
Sunday. A coworker posts a photo from the office in the group chat: “Anyone else here?” You’re at the country house. Your move?
You planned to work out, eat breakfast, and read. You woke up ten minutes before you had to leave. Your choice?
At lunch, a coworker shares that he learned Spanish with an app in six months. You downloaded the same app and quit after a day. Your choice?
Friday, 6 p.m. You promised yourself not to open work email this weekend. It has already pinged twice. What now?
You decided this morning: leave at six sharp and go swimming. At 9:15, your lead books a meeting at 5:30. Your move?
Your fitness app reproachfully notes you’ve walked 400 steps today. It’s 3 p.m., and most of those were to the coffee machine. What do you say?
You started a time-management podcast to find time for hobbies. It’s three hours long. Your reaction?
right: Turn it off and go for a walk

text: You’ve slept five hours a night for a week. Today’s an important meeting, and you’re nodding off on the subway. Buy an energy drink?
A coworker suggests signing up for pottery classes together on Thursdays — the only evening you usually make it to the store. What now?
Saturday, 11:40 p.m. Your lead liked an old vacation photo of yours on social media. What could that mean?
The office got an exercise bike with a laptop stand: “Work and slim down.” It’s free. Try it?
You decided to walk every lunch to clear your head. Today it’s pouring, and coworkers all invite you to the cafeteria. What do you do?
Evening. You scroll social media where everyone’s traveling, running marathons, and baking bread. You ate instant noodles over the sink. Your move?
Sunday morning. You woke up refreshed for the first time in a month. Do something for yourself, or prep for the week?
The company chat announces a 5K run on Saturday morning. Participation is “voluntary, but highly encouraged.” What now?
Monday morning. You woke up tired even after nine hours of sleep. The thought of the office makes you want to become a cactus. What now?
Brushing your teeth, you realize you haven’t smiled before lunch for three days straight. Your reflection looks like a quarterly report. Your move?
You realize you’re on your fourth coffee before 10 a.m. and still rereading the same sentence for the fifth time. What do you say?
You rode past your stop because you were lost in work thoughts. Again. Third time this week. Your reaction?
A coworker remarks: “You’ve seemed kind of colorless lately.” You sense it’s not about your sweater. Talk about it?
7:10 a.m. Twenty messages in the work chat already, though the workday starts at nine. You’re still in bed. Read them?
You’ve stood at the office door for five minutes and can’t go in. Your legs won’t move. Security is eyeing you. What now?
The alarm rings, and you dream of an illness that would legally let you stay home. Nothing serious, just a week’s worth. Warning sign?
Your lead asks why you’ve been silent at stand-up for three days. You used to at least joke. What do you say?
You open your calendar and find your last work-free day off was six weeks ago. Request a day off?
You fell asleep on the bus and woke up repeating “Yes, I’ll have it by lunch.” Your neighbor looks at you with sympathy. What do you do?
Saturday morning. A coworker writes: “Can you check one number in the report? Five minutes.” You just made coffee. Your move?
You notice you don’t care whether you get praised or scolded today. You used to care. Your choice?
HR sends a survey: “How do you feel at work?” Options range from “great” to “very good.” Your answer is “nothing.” What now?
Your lead suggests you “spearhead a new initiative,” since you’re so responsible. You’re already swamped. Your move?
Sunday morning. You woke up from dreaming you were answering an email. You want to check you didn’t actually send it. What do you do?
In the morning, a coworker leaves a chocolate bar and a note: “You’re holding up great.” You nearly cry at your desk. Your reaction?
Today’s to-do list is longer than the workday. You add one more item: “don’t lose your mind.” What now?
You woke up thinking “What’s the point of all this?” The kettle boiled, but no answer. What do you do with this morning?
Your mentor pulls you aside: “Listen, you look completely worn out. Take a day off, I’ll cover.” Accept?
Your lead suggests coming in Saturday “for half a day” to tie up loose ends. He promises “a day off sometime later.” What do you do?
You’ve stared at a spreadsheet for twenty minutes and haven’t done a single thing. Your brain just refuses. Your move?
Friday, 9 p.m. Your lead writes: “Have a great weekend! P.S. Need the report Monday at 9:00.” It’s not started. Your choice?
You got home, sat on the hallway floor, and stayed there twenty minutes without taking off your jacket. Sound familiar?
11:15 p.m. A coworker posts “good night” in the group chat, followed by twenty project questions. Answer?
Sunday, 8 p.m. A message from your lead: “Can you come in early tomorrow?” No explanation. What now?
You notice you no longer look forward to weekends: you just lie there dreading Monday. Time for a change?
At home, they say you’ve become irritable and always on your phone. You’re on your phone right now. Your move?
Friday, 6:05 p.m. Jacket on, and an email arrives: “Not urgent, but if you get it done today, that’d be great.” What do you say?
Third evening in a row you’re having chips for dinner because you’re too drained to cook. The fridge looks at you reproachfully. Your reaction?
You turned off your work phone for the weekend for the first time in a month. On Monday: 47 missed calls. Your move?
Saturday night at the movies with friends, and your lead writes: “Urgent! Call me.” It’s the best part of the film. What now?
On your day off, you catch yourself ironing shirts and mentally rehearsing Monday’s stand-up. Stop?
A coworker texts in the evening: “I think I’m burning out. How about you?” You stare at the message for a long time, not knowing what to say. What do you do?
You promised yourself not to open the laptop after eight. It’s 8:01. Notification: “You were mentioned.” Your move?
In the evening you suddenly cry at a yogurt commercial. It’s not the yogurt or the ad. You’re just very, very tired. What do you do?
Four months till vacation. Every evening you count the days on a calculator. Today: 121. Your choice?
Your lead notices you’ve stayed late all week and says: “Great job, but go home.” How do you respond?
Sunday, 10 p.m. A coworker forwards a client email: “First thing in the morning.” You’re about to sleep. What now?
In the evening you realize you can’t remember the last time you laughed. Not a polite smile — really laughed. Your move?
Friday, 7 p.m. Everyone’s gone, and you’re sitting in the empty office, unsure why you stayed. Nothing left for today. What do you say?
Mom writes in the family chat: “You’ve kind of disappeared. Everything okay?” You type “yes” and delete it. Your reaction?
You got home, lay on the couch, and realized you’d had your shoulders up by your ears all day. They ache. Do something?
Friday, 11:30 p.m. Your lead sends a Monday meme captioned “Get ready.” Funny?
Evening. You opened a job site “just to look” and spent two hours there. No applications sent. What now?
A friend sends a “Are You Burned Out?” quiz. You maxed out every item. What do you do?
You catch yourself checking work email at the theater during intermission. The play is about the meaning of life. Your move?
Sunday evening. You’re meal-prepping for the week, ironing shirts, and planning the day. Is this self-care or battle prep?
At the end of the day, your lead asks how you’re doing. First time in three months. You’re not ready for that question. Your choice?
Friday. The week is over, and you survived. No energy to celebrate, but you made it. How do you mark it?
